data.title: Event Logs Can Be Cleared Without Alerting
data.summary:
Windows event logs were cleared on compromised hosts. Because logs are retained locally
and not forwarded, the record of the intrusion was destroyed and no alert was generated by
the clearing itself.
data.description:
Local-only logging makes the evidence of an intrusion destructible by the intrusion. An
attacker who reaches administrative rights can remove the record of how they got there,
and the organisation loses the ability to scope the incident — which matters more, in
practice, than losing the ability to detect it.

Log clearing is itself a high-fidelity signal. It generates a distinctive event, it has
very few legitimate causes, and it is among the most reliable alerts available. Acting on
it requires that logs be forwarded off the host in near real time, so that the forwarded
copy survives.

Command history suppression belongs in the same finding: a shell configured not to record
what was run leaves the same gap on Unix hosts.
data.recommendation:
* Forward logs off the host in near real time so the authoritative copy is outside the
  attacker's reach.
* Alert on log clearing and on the audit service being stopped; both have few legitimate
  causes.
* Retain forwarded logs for a period matched to realistic dwell time rather than to the
  default local size limit.
* Monitor for command history suppression on Unix hosts.
data.short_recommendation: Forward logs off-host in real time and alert on clearing.
